rv.q: It’s the raciest, rudest, most rip-roaringly funny show in town.
Park makes her as riveting as a tractor beam.
Wickedly camp, outrageous and ridiculously funny
Escola’s play basically sits in a genre of its own, one that mixes the farcical humour of am-dram classics like Charley’s Aunt with the disturbing queer energy of early John Waters films.

Park’s Mary is riveting, and just as watchable during fiery exchanges with her husband (a no-nonsense Giles Terera), as in giddy lessons with her acting teacher (Dino Fetscher) and when bullying her chaperone (Kate O’Donnell).

Again directed by Sam Pinkleton, this knowingly bogus portrait of the First Lady as a dipsomaniac and frustrated cabaret star is a riot, laced with a truth about the necessity of self-expression, in which American actor Mason Alexander Park gives the funniest performance in town.
All the silliness is maddeningly insistent, never yielding to subtext and sincerity.
But that’s not the same thing as living up to the hype.
Show is loaded with obvious jokes with American Pie-levels of puerile humour.
But, honestly, the script and the jokes remain ridiculously thin.
Not only fake news, it’s fake entertainment.
I couldn't twist my mouth into a smile at any point, let alone laugh.
Oh, Mary! is daft, daring and meticulously put together.
And following their stand-out performances in Jamie Lloyd’s recent Shakespearean double, The Tempest (as Ariel) and About Nothing, Park knocks Mary out of the park.
Outrageous and iconoclastic, Oh Mary! is queer, delicious fun.
That really sums up this entertaining romp: it’s a wildly unlikely sensation.
The most contentious elements in the show are also the ones which cause the greatest surprise and loudest laughs.
Oh, Mary! offers something genuinely different: a comedy that is as unpredictable as it is audacious.
It’s silly, irreverent, and utterly irresistible, full of shocks and surprises.
This amazing climax arrives 65 minutes into the show but the rest of it has no drive or purpose.
I suspect this will prove to be a divisive production; those who love it will adore it, but there will be those who may shrug and wonder what all the fuss is about.
But knowing how ‘hot’ this piece of dreary rubbish was on Broadway, I left a lot more worried about America’s future than before.

cn.t: Critics mostly embrace this outrageous Broadway import as gleefully silly and unlike anything else, praising its camp excess and Mason Alexander Park's star turn, though a few dismiss it as cringe-making overacting and tasteless nonsense.
